criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Identifies three significant issues, links design trade to ethics, explains organisational context of calendar-driven testing and conflict of interest, and details six stakeholders with interests and decisions in Table 1.

evidence.quote: test coverage is being set by the release calendar instead of by risk

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Presents objective depth on both sides with commercial, learning and harm arguments, then draws differentiated conclusions and tailored decision recommendations for Rachel, management, health department and supplier.

evidence.quote: Shipping on time protects a real competitive advantage.
The strongest objection is harm to people who have no say.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logical flow from for/against to risk-based decision rule in Figure 1 and Table 2 options analysis, compellingly justifying withhold sign-off conclusion with systematic stakeholder consideration.

evidence.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?
evidence.quote: Neither "never ship a defect" nor "ship unless someone could be physically hurt" is adequate.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Eight reputable sources including Engineers Australia, AS ISO 31000, NAO, Leveson, HBR, Intel, DOJ. Quantitative evidence on cancellations, costs, penalties plus qualitative ethical analysis shows balanced in-depth research.

evidence.quote: at least 81 of 236 hospital trusts in England were disrupted
National Audit Office, "Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS," HC 414

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Includes abstract, introduction, body, conclusion and recommendations; fluent concise language; competent Table 1, Table 2 and Figure 1; consistent IEEE-style references supporting motivations.

evidence.quote: Table 1: Stakeholders, their interests and the decision each controls.

overall: Exceptional holistic report meeting all tasks. Well-argued risk-informed recommendation with strong evidence, stakeholder coverage, and professional presentation.

feedback.summary: You produced an exceptional, well-argued report with a clear risk-informed recommendation. You linked design trade-offs to ethics, balanced commercial and harm arguments, and supported every claim with strong evidence and professional presentation. To stay at this level, maintain this depth, stakeholder focus, and structure in future work.
next_steps: Continue using risk-based decision tools like your Figure 1 to make your recommendations auditable for all stakeholders.
Keep integrating quantitative impact data with qualitative ethical analysis to sustain research depth.
Maintain your clear tables and stakeholder-specific recommendations to keep arguments compelling and actionable.
